title: In Great Britain, cost of living and public services remain dominant concerns while drought turns climate concern into everyday water conservation
source_unit: UK Office for National Statistics, Public opinions and social trends, Great Britain: August 2026, released 18 September 2026
geography: Adults in England, Scotland, and Wales surveyed through the ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey

cost_of_living.unit: percent identifying cost of living as an important issue facing the UK

nhs.unit: percent identifying the NHS as an important issue

economy.unit: percent identifying the economy as an important issue

public_priority_route.value: cost, health-system capacity, and the economy remain the dominant public problem frame

observations.method: ONS statistical bulletin based on the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey for adults in Great Britain.
observations.uncertainty: Issue-priority responses are descriptive public opinion, not measures of policy effectiveness, objective service performance, or a causal ranking of national problems.
observations.subgroup: Adults across England, Scotland, and Wales, households facing cost pressures, NHS users, workers, and policymakers.
observations.counterinterpretation: High issue salience can reflect media attention, recent events, or broad concern and does not imply uniform personal exposure or a single policy preference.

observations.period: June-August 2026; climate and environment as a public issue

climate_environment.unit: percent identifying climate change and the environment as an important issue in August

june_comparison.unit: percent identifying climate change and the environment as an important issue in June

late_2024_comparison.value: the August proportion is the highest reported since late 2024

climate_voice_route.value: climate salience has risen within a public agenda still dominated by cost, health, and economic concerns

observations.method: ONS repeated public-opinion indicators comparing August 2026 with June 2026 and earlier releases.
observations.uncertainty: Issue salience does not reveal preferred climate policy, willingness to bear costs, personal exposure, or whether concern persists after drought conditions change.
observations.subgroup: Adults in Great Britain, households exposed to drought, climate-concerned publics, and people balancing environmental and cost priorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising climate salience may be event-driven by drought and water restrictions rather than a durable shift in values or political behavior.

observations.period: 5-30 August 2026; drought, water restrictions, and household adaptation

any_water_action.unit: percent reporting at least one action to cut back household water use in the past month

tap_action.unit: percent reporting not leaving the tap running

full_load_action.unit: percent waiting until washing machines or dishwashers were full

garden_action.unit: percent using less tap water, including hosepipes, in the garden, up from 36 percent in July

adaptation_route.value: drought and restrictions translated climate and infrastructure pressure into visible household routines

observations.method: ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey indicators on reported water-use actions during August 2026 drought and restriction conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Reported actions do not measure water volumes saved, persistence, costs, unequal burden, or the effectiveness of restrictions; respondents could select multiple actions.
observations.subgroup: Households in Great Britain, adults in areas with and without restrictions, women and men, and younger and older adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Short-term conservation can be event-driven and may not persist without infrastructure, pricing, communication, or institutional support.

observations.period: 5-30 August 2026; cost-of-living pressure and household tradeoffs

cost_increase.unit: percent reporting their cost of living increased compared with one month earlier

food_reason.unit: percent of those reporting an increase citing food-shopping prices

fuel_reason.unit: percent of those reporting an increase citing fuel prices

energy_reason.unit: percent of those reporting an increase citing gas or electricity bills

tradeoff_route.value: households most commonly responded by cutting non-essentials, shopping around, and reducing food shopping or essentials

open_test.value: connect public issue salience to actual household room, health, energy, food, and political response without treating survey shares as individual histories

observations.method: ONS repeated cross-sectional indicators on reported cost changes, sources of increases, and household actions.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are self-reported and conditional; they do not estimate household budgets, price elasticities, poverty transitions, or causal effects of specific costs.
observations.subgroup: Households with different ages, incomes, food and energy burdens, workers, and consumers across Great Britain.
observations.counterinterpretation: The decline in reported monthly cost increases from April does not mean cost pressure has disappeared; households may have adapted or expectations may have changed.

related_sources.claim: ONS water-restrictions dataset provides the related August 2026 downloadable indicators and confidence intervals.
ONS June 2026 release provides prior climate-salience and AI-attitudes comparison context.

boundary: This record adds a Great Britain public-opinion route from cost, health-system, and economic concern through climate salience, drought adaptation, water use, and household tradeoffs. It uses official aggregate survey indicators, not respondent-level records in the corpus, causal household histories, water-volume measurement, or proof that salience produces durable policy action.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ONS August 2026 statistical bulletin was reviewed for issue priorities, climate salience, water-use actions, restriction awareness, cost-of-living change, cost drivers, and household responses.
